I pick **candidate 0**. This was worked out in my head, not simulated, and the lead over candidates 6 and 1 is small.

1. **Plans that lose clearly:**
   - **Candidate 7** orders almost every day. That costs about 28 × 49 ≈ 1370 in daily order fees, against 441 for plans that order every 3 days. Its lower storage costs don't make up the difference.
   - **Candidate 2** orders every 4 days in large batches (85 + 84). By about day 3 the stock passes the 148-unit limit, so some delivered units, already paid for, are lost.
   - **Candidate 4** orders about 23% above average demand. Leftovers build up, and at product 0 deliveries the stock is likely to hit 148, so units are lost there too.

2. **Ordering every 2 days (candidates 3 and 6) against every 3 days (candidates 0, 1, 5):** ordering every 2 days costs 5 × 49 = 245 more in order fees. It saves roughly 0.4 × 17 units × 27 days ≈ 190 in storage. Every 3 days comes out slightly ahead.

3. **Choosing among the every-3-days plans:**
   - A missing unit costs about 10 (lost margin of 8 plus the penalty of 2 for product 0; 9 plus 2 for product 1).
   - A leftover unit costs very little. It mostly costs about 1.2 in storage, because it is sold first in the next cycle and rarely expires.
   - So ordering a little above the average is worth it. Candidate 0 does that (about 1.1 × average demand), stays clear of the 148 limit, and is more robust than candidates 5 and 1, which order at about the average for product 0.

**Ответ: кандидат 0.** Расчёты я делал в уме и проверил вручную только первые дни, поэтому уверенность средняя.

**Затраты на заказы.** Каждый день с заказом стоит 49, поэтому частые заказы съедают прибыль.
- **Кандидат 7** заказывает почти каждый день: около 28 × 49 ≈ 1370 на одни заказы. Это слишком много при марже 8–9 за единицу и общем спросе около 1050 единиц.
- **Кандидаты 3 и 6** заказывают раз в 2 дня: 14 × 49 = 686. Это примерно на 245 дороже, чем заказы раз в 3 дня (9 × 49 = 441). Меньший запас экономит на хранении примерно 180 или меньше, так что разницу это не покрывает.

**Почему выигрывает цикл в 3 дня (кандидаты 0, 1, 4, 5).** Товар 0 продаётся 5 дней, а следующая поставка приходит через 3. Значит, остаток партии продаётся в начале следующего цикла (сначала идут старые партии), и лишнее количество обходится в основном хранением, а не списанием. Если не хватает, теряется маржа плюс неустойка: около 10–11 за единицу. Поэтому разумно заказывать на 10–20 % больше прогноза.

Сравнение заказа с прогнозным спросом за цикл:

| Кандидат | Товар 0 | Товар 1 | Что не так |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | ≈ 1,15 | ≈ 1,14 | — |
| 1 | ≈ 1,06 | ≈ 1,19 | товара 0 мало при среднем множителе 1,046 и неустойке |
| 4 | ≈ 1,30 | ≈ 1,30 | излишек копится примерно по 13 ед. за цикл и списывается; уже в день 6 склад переполняется (155 > 148, пропадает 7 ед.) |
| 5 | ≈ 1,06 | ≈ 1,05 | частые нехватки, если спрос выше прогноза |

**Кандидат 2** (цикл в 4 дня) экономит около 2 заказов (≈ 98). Но остатки товара 0 почти не успевают дожить до следующей поставки, а большие партии переполняют склад, например в день 3 (153 > 148).

**Устойчивость к случайному спросу.** У кандидата 0 запас около 15 % на обоих товарах. Это прикрывает от нехваток, когда спрос выше прогноза, но не превращается в массовые списания, когда спрос ниже. Для фактического спроса, который колеблется примерно на ±30 %, такой баланс устойчивее остальных.

I picked candidate 0. I worked this out by hand with rough figures, not a full day-by-day simulation, so it's an estimate. These are the main factors:

1. **Fixed cost of ordering (49 per day with an order).**
   - Candidate 7 orders every day, about 28 orders, costing about 1370. That costs far more than it can recover.
   - Candidates 3 and 6 order every 2 days, about 14 orders, costing about 690.
   - Candidates 0, 1, 4 and 5 order every 3 days: 9 orders, 441.
   - Candidate 2 orders every 4 days: 7 orders, 343.
2. **Candidate 2.** It saves only about 98 in order fees compared with the 3-day plans, but it loses more than that.
   - Its batches are larger, so average stock is higher. Extra storage across both products comes to roughly 200 or more over the 30 days.
   - The warehouse already overflows on day 3: about 68 units of product 1 are still in stock when 85 units of product 0 arrive. That is 153 units against a limit of 148.
3. **Choosing among the 3-day plans (0, 1, 4, 5).** Expected demand is the forecast × 1.046.
   - **Product 0.** Expected demand over the delivery period (days 3–29) is about 468 units. A unit can only be sold for 5 days, so not much is left over for the next delivery. Running out costs about 10 per unit (lost margin 8 plus penalty 2). That justifies a small safety margin of a few units per delivery.
     - Candidates 1 and 5 order 470 in total, which is just the average and leaves no margin.
     - Candidate 4 orders 575, about 107 extra units that will mostly spoil.
     - Candidate 0 orders 509, about +5 units per delivery, which is close to the right margin.
   - **Product 1.** Expected demand is about 510 units. It keeps for 8 days, so unsold stock carries over to the next delivery and only a modest total margin is needed.
     - Candidate 0 orders 553 (+43), which is reasonable.
     - Candidate 4 orders 625 (+115), which is clearly too much: about 1380 in purchase cost alone for units that won't sell.
     - Candidate 5 orders 509, exactly the average, so it will often run short when demand varies.

Candidate 0 has the low order cost of a 3-day schedule and sensible safety margins on both products. It should hold up best when actual demand differs from the forecast, so it has the highest expected profit.

I worked this out by reasoning rather than simulating every day, so this is a judgement call, not an exact calculation. I pick **plan 0**.

- **Plans 7, 3 and 6 lose too much on order fees.** Plan 7 orders on 28 days, which costs 49 × 28 = 1372 in fees. Plans 3 and 6 order every second day, about 14 times (686). Ordering every third day (plans 0, 1, 4 and 5) costs about 9 × 49 = 441. Holding less stock in the every-second-day plans doesn't make up the 245 difference.
- **Plan 2 is ruled out by warehouse space.** It orders every fourth day, and its deliveries of 85 and 84 add up to 169 against 148 places. The two items arrive on different days, but stock left from earlier deliveries pushes the warehouse over capacity, so some paid-for units are lost.
- **Choosing among the every-third-day plans:**
  - A shortage costs about 10–11 per unit (the lost margin of 8–9 plus the 2 penalty).
  - A surplus is cheap. Item 0 keeps for 5 days and item 1 for 8, so leftovers carry into the next cycle.
  - That favours ordering a bit above expected demand. Expected demand is about 56 units for item 0 per cycle and about 60 for item 1.
  - Plan 5 orders about at expected demand, so it runs short too often. Plan 1 does the same for item 0.
  - Plan 4 orders well above demand (+14 per cycle for item 1). The extra stock builds up, which raises the risk of spoilage and overflow.
  - Plan 0 orders about 5–6 units above expected demand for both items. That makes it the best balance.

I'd pick **candidate 0**. I estimated this in my head without simulating, so it's a judgement call rather than an exact calculation.

1. **How often to order.** The fixed cost is 49 per order day. Ordering every day (candidate 7) costs about 1 370 in fixed fees. Ordering every 2 days (candidates 3 and 6) costs about 690. Ordering every 3 days (candidates 0, 1, 4, 5) costs about 440, and a 3-day cycle fits within the 5-day shelf life of product 0.
2. **Why not every 4 days (candidate 2).** It saves only about 150 in fees. But with batches of around 85 + 84 units, a product 0 delivery arrives when roughly 68 units of product 1 are still in stock. That totals about 153 units before counting leftovers, so the 148-unit warehouse overflows and the excess is lost.
3. **How much to order.** A missed sale costs about 10–11 per unit (lost margin plus penalty). An extra unit costs much less: it mostly sells in the next cycle, and storage is 0.4 per day. Demand averages 1.046 × forecast, and over 3 days it varies by about 17%. So the best order size is roughly 1.15–1.25 × the forecast for the period.
   - Candidate 5 is about 1.05×, so it runs short.
   - Candidate 1 is about 1.05× for product 0 and 1.2× for product 1.
   - Candidate 0 is about 1.15× for both products.
   - Candidate 4 is about 1.3×. Its surplus builds up, so it gets close to the warehouse limit and more stock spoils.

Candidate 0 is the most balanced. Candidate 1 is the closest alternative.

I picked **candidate 1**. I worked this out without running a simulation, so treat it as a reasoned estimate, not a verified result.

1. **Three-day cycle.** Candidates 0, 1, 4 and 5 order every 3 days. That costs 9 order fees of 49, compared with 14 for the 2-day plans and 28 for the daily plan. Product 0 keeps for 5 days, which covers a 3-day batch with time to spare.
2. **Product 0 order size.** Running out of a unit costs the lost margin of 8 plus the penalty of 2, so about 10. A unit left over goes off at a loss of about 7 plus storage. That points to stocking around 4–8 % above the forecast, which matches candidate 1's ×1.05.
3. **Product 1 order size.** It keeps for 8 days, so leftovers carry into the next cycle and mostly cost only storage. Running out costs about 11. So it is worth stocking well above the forecast, and candidate 1's ×1.2 fits.
4. **Warehouse limit of 148.** Candidates 0 and 4 order large amounts of product 0 before the demand spike on day 14, so some deliveries would likely be lost to overflow. In candidate 1 the two products arrive on different days. Around day 12, stock comes to roughly 80 + 46 + leftovers ≈ 136, which is under the limit.

I picked **candidate 0**. This is a mental estimate, not a simulation.

- **Order frequency:** Every order day costs 49. Candidate 7 orders almost daily, so it pays about 1,370 in fees, which wipes out most of the margin. Ordering every 3 days costs about 440 for 9 orders. The 2-day plans (3 and 6) cost about 735. Ordering every 3 days does mean holding more stock, which adds roughly 200 in storage. The extra ~300 in fees for the 2-day plans is larger, so the 3-day plans come out slightly ahead.
- **Choosing among the 3-day plans (0, 1, 4, 5):**
  - Order sizes: candidate 0's batches sit about half a standard deviation above expected demand per cycle (expected demand already includes the ×1.046 multiplier). That's reasonable because a shortage loses about 8–9 in margin plus the 2 penalty. Leftovers are cheap: product 1 keeps for 8 days and product 0 can still sell in the next cycle.
  - Candidate 1 orders less product 0 than expected demand.
  - Candidate 5 orders less product 1.
  - Candidate 4 orders more than needed and is closer to the 148-unit storage limit.
- **Candidate 2 (every 4 days):** Its batches are large, and stock peaks close to 148. Anything over the limit is lost even though it's already paid for.

I estimate **candidate 0** has the highest expected profit. I worked through the comparison mentally without simulating it, so this is a judgement, not an exact calculation.

- **Order frequency:** ordering every day (candidate 7) costs about 28 × 49 ≈ 1,370 in fees, which wipes out what it saves on storage. Ordering every 4 days (candidate 2) brings in large batches. Those risk overflowing the 148-unit warehouse, and product 0 can spoil because it only sells for 5 days. That leaves the plans that order every 3 days (candidates 0, 1, 4, 5) or every 2 days (candidates 3, 6).
- **Every 2 days vs every 3 days:** ordering every 2 days adds about 5 more order days, costing about 245 more. It saves roughly 190 in storage plus a little in safety stock. That makes the two close, with a slight edge to ordering every 3 days.
- **Choosing among the every-3-days plans:** a missed sale costs about 10–11 per unit: the lost margin of 8–9 plus the penalty of 2. A unit left over costs only storage, because product 0 can still sell for 2 more days and product 1 for 8. So ordering slightly above the forecast pays off.
  - Candidate 1 orders product 0 at the expected 3-day demand, about 57 units, so it would run short about half the time.
  - Candidate 5 does the same for product 1, at about 60 units.
  - Candidate 4 orders about 23% above demand, which builds up stock, wastes product 0 and gets close to the warehouse limit.
  - Candidate 0 orders about 9% above expected demand for both products. That is roughly half to one standard deviation of the 3-day demand, which is the right amount of buffer.

I picked **Candidate 0**. I estimated expected profit by hand, as you asked: no code was run and nothing was simulated. Candidates 0, 6 and 1 are close, so this is a judgement call.

**How often to order.** Each day you order costs a fixed 49, so ordering more often costs more but keeps less stock on the shelf.
- **Candidate 7** orders almost every day, 28 orders in all. That is about 1,372 in fixed costs, roughly 930 more than the 3-day plans. The lower holding cost does not make up for this.
- **Candidates 3 and 6** order every 2 days, 14 orders in all. That is about 245 more in fixed costs than the 3-day plans. Stock on hand is lower by about half a day's demand per product, which saves about 0.4 × 18 × 27 ≈ 195 in holding. That leaves them about 50 behind, so a 3-day cycle comes out slightly better.
- **Candidate 2** orders every 4 days, which saves only 98 in fixed costs. The bigger stock adds about 240 in holding. The 148-unit storage limit is also exceeded, for example on day 3 (68 of product 1 + 85 of product 0 = 153), and on day 11, so some delivered units are lost.

**How much to order (candidates 0, 1, 4, 5, all on a 3-day cycle).** I compared each order with expected demand over the days it covers, using forecast × 1.046.
- Product 0: running out costs about 10 per unit (lost margin 8 plus penalty 2). Leftovers keep only 5 days, so a big surplus gets written off at 7 per unit.
- Product 1: running out costs about 11 per unit. Leftovers keep 8 days and carry into the next cycle, but a steady surplus still ends up written off at 12 per unit.

For each candidate, order size as a share of expected demand:
- **Candidate 4** orders about 1.24× for both products. Surplus builds up and gets written off, and on day 12 it slightly exceeds storage (about 52 + 99 = 151).
- **Candidate 5** orders about 1.0× for both. It runs short too often given the roughly 18% swing in demand over a 3-day period.
- **Candidate 1** orders about 1.0× for product 0 and about 1.14× for product 1. That is too little of the first and too much of the second.
- **Candidate 0** orders about 1.1× for product 0 and about 1.09× for product 1. That is a reasonable buffer for both products, and its last orders (44 and 60) closely match end-of-month demand, so little is wasted at the end.

**Robustness.** If actual demand moves away from forecast, Candidate 0 keeps a moderate buffer and never exceeds storage. It loses less to shortages than candidates 5 and 1, and less to write-offs than 4 and 2.

I worked this out by reasoning rather than simulating it, so **candidate 0** is my best estimate, not a verified result.

1. **Fixed order cost.** Each day with an order costs 49.
   - Ordering every day (candidate 7) costs about 1,370, which is far too much.
   - Ordering every 2 days (candidates 3 and 6) costs about 690.
   - Ordering every 3 days (candidates 0, 1, 4 and 5) costs about 440.
   - Ordering every 4 days (candidate 2) is cheaper, but each batch is about 85 + 85 units against a 148-unit warehouse. With random demand spikes, some stock is likely to be lost on arrival, and holding costs are higher.

2. **Every 3 days fits the delivery times.** Item 0 arrives after 3 days and item 1 after 2, so the two items arrive on different days. A 3-day batch of item 0 also fits within its 5-day shelf life.

3. **Order size among the 3-day plans.** For the first batch I compared the order with forecast demand over the days it covers. Item 0 covers days 3–5, with 54 forecast. Item 1 covers days 2–4, with 57 forecast.
   - Candidates 1 and 5 order about 1.05× forecast. That is roughly average demand, since the multiplier averages about 1.046, so they would often run short.
   - Candidate 4 orders about 1.3× forecast. Stock would build up, risking warehouse overflow, item 0 spoiling and extra holding costs.
   - Candidate 0 orders about 1.15× forecast, about half a standard deviation above average 3-day demand.

4. **Why lean high.** A missed sale loses the margin plus the shortage penalty: 8 + 2 = 10 for item 0, and 9 + 2 = 11 for item 1. A leftover unit usually costs only a little holding, because it can still be sold in the next days. So it pays to order somewhat above average, but not so much that stock builds up.

Я выбираю **кандидата 1**, но уверенность средняя. Всё считал в уме и только приблизительно. Разница между кандидатами 0 и 1 небольшая и зависит от того, как будет вести себя случайный спрос.

**Постоянные расходы на заказы (49 за каждый день с заказом):**
- Кандидат 7 заказывает 28 дней из 30, это около 1372. Такой расход съедает заметную часть маржи (8 на товаре 0 и 9 на товаре 1), поэтому план слабый.
- Кандидаты 3 и 6 заказывают через день, это около 14 заказов, примерно 686. Получается на ~245 дороже, чем при цикле в 3 дня. Небольшой выигрыш в страховом запасе эту разницу не покрывает.
- Кандидат 2 заказывает раз в 4 дня (7 заказов, около 343), но партии слишком большие для склада. Например, утром дня 3 на складе уже около 68 ед. товара 1 из партии в 84, которая пришла в день 2. Вместе с приходящими 85 ед. товара 0 получается больше 148, и излишек пропадает. Пропажи и списания перекрывают экономию в ~98.
- Кандидаты 0, 1, 4 и 5 заказывают раз в 3 дня (9 заказов, около 441). Это лучшая частота.

**Объёмы заказов при цикле в 3 дня.** Средний спрос — это прогноз × 1,046.
- **Товар 0** (годность 5 дней). Партия из дня 0 покрывает дни 3–5: средний спрос около 56,5. Кандидаты 1 и 5 заказывают 57, то есть ровно в среднее. Кандидат 0 заказывает 62, а кандидат 4 — 70. Постоянный перезаказ копится, и с годностью 5 дней излишек списывается. Всплеск в день 14 (прогноз 43) у кандидата 1 покрыт: заказ 80 при среднем спросе за дни 12–14 около 79,5.
- **Товар 1** (годность 8 дней). Нехватка единицы стоит 11 (маржа 9 + неустойка 2). Лишняя единица дешёвая: она переходит в следующий цикл, и за 3 дня хранения платится всего 1,2. Поэтому выгодно заказывать с запасом выше среднего. Партия из дня 0 покрывает дни 2–4: средний спрос около 59,6. Кандидат 1 заказывает 68, это разумный страховой запас. У кандидата 5 (60) почти нет запаса, поэтому при случайном спросе он чаще упирается в нехватку. Кандидат 4 (70/74) рискует переполнить склад и терять товар 0 на списаниях.

**Итог.** Кандидат 1 держит товар 0 на уровне среднего спроса, а товар 1 — с умеренным запасом. Поэтому при отклонениях спроса от прогноза его ожидаемая прибыль должна быть самой высокой. Ближайший соперник — кандидат 0.

I'd pick **candidate 0**. I estimated this in my head without simulating it, so it's a judgement call, not a computed optimum.

1. **Ordering every day is too expensive (candidate 7).** It places orders on 28 days, so the fixed fees alone are about 49 × 28 ≈ 1370. The every-third-day plans pay only about 8 × 49 ≈ 390.
2. **Ordering every fourth day hits the space limit (candidate 2).** A single delivery of about 85 + 84 units, plus leftover stock, can go over the 148-unit capacity, and the excess is lost. Item 0 also keeps only 5 days, so a 4-day cycle risks spoilage.
3. **Among the every-third-day plans (0, 1, 4, 5), slightly over-ordering is better.**
   - Running out costs more than having extra. A missed unit of item 0 loses about 10 (8 margin + 2 penalty). A missed unit of item 1 loses about 11.
   - Extra stock is cheap. Leftovers mostly sell in the next cycle, and storage is 0.4 per unit per day. Item 1 keeps 8 days, so its leftovers are rarely written off.
   - Expected demand for one cycle is about 54 units per item (forecast × 1.046), with a spread of roughly ±10.
   - Candidates 1 and 5 order close to the mean, which risks running out.
   - Candidate 4 orders about 1.2 spreads above the mean (65 and 70). That raises storage costs and leaves more unsold stock at the end of the 30 days.
   - Candidate 0 orders about 0.4 spreads above the mean (58 and 62), and its last orders roughly match end-of-horizon demand (44 and 60). That looks like the best balance.

I picked **candidate 5**. I worked this out by hand with rough estimates rather than running a full simulation.

**Fixed ordering costs.** Each day with an order costs 49.
- Candidate 7 orders almost every day, about 28 times, so it pays about 1,370 in fees. That is clearly worst.
- Candidates 3 and 6 order every 2 days: 14 orders, about 686.
- Candidates 0, 1, 4 and 5 order every 3 days: 9 orders, about 441.
- Candidate 2 orders every 4 days: 7 orders, about 343. But it brings in large batches (85/84, 95/75 and so on). That means a lot of storage cost, and product 0 lasts only 5 days, so it risks spoiling.

**How totals compare with expected demand.** I added up the forecast for the days the orders actually cover and multiplied by 1.046, the average demand multiplier.
- Product 0 (days 3–29) needs about 468. Candidates 1 and 5 order 470, candidate 0 orders 509 and candidate 4 orders 575.
- Product 1 (days 2–29) needs about 510. Candidate 5 orders 509, candidate 0 orders 553, candidate 1 orders 579 and candidate 4 orders 625.

**Over-ordering versus under-ordering.**
- A unit short costs about 8–9 in lost margin plus a 2 penalty, so about 10–11.
- An extra unit costs 7–12 to buy plus storage, and stock left at the end is worth nothing.
- Leftovers carry over into the next cycle (product 1 lasts 8 days), so a buffer mostly ends up as unsold stock at the end.
- Because those two costs are about equal, it pays to order close to expected demand. Candidate 4 over-orders by about 100 units of each product, which loses well over 1,000. Candidates 0 and 1 also lose money on their surplus.

**Candidate 3 versus candidate 5.** Candidate 3 also matches expected demand and orders every 2 days. Its smaller batches save roughly 190 in storage and slightly cut shortages and spoilage. That does not cover its extra 245 in ordering fees, so candidate 5 comes out a little ahead.

Я выбрал **кандидата 5** — у него наибольший ожидаемый итог. Расчёт примерный, в уме.

1. **Частота заказов.** Каждый день с заказом стоит 49.
   - Кандидат 7 заказывает 28 дней подряд, это около 1372. Он заведомо худший.
   - Кандидаты 3 и 6 заказывают раз в 2 дня, всего 14 раз, это 686. Против цикла в 3 дня (9 раз, 441) они переплачивают около 245. Экономия на хранении при этом примерно 18 ед. × 0,4 × 27 дн. ≈ 195, то есть меньше.
   - Кандидат 2 заказывает раз в 4 дня, всего 7 раз, это 343. Он экономит 98, но средний запас у него выше примерно на 18 ед., и хранение обходится дороже на ~200. Кроме того, склад на 148 ед. переполняется, например в дни 3 и 7.

   Лучше всего цикл в 3 дня, то есть кандидаты 0, 1, 4 и 5.

2. **Объём заказов против ожидаемого спроса.** Ожидаемый спрос (прогноз × 1,046), который покрывают поставки, такой:
   - товар 0 (дни 3–29): около 468;
   - товар 1 (дни 2–29): около 510.

   | Кандидат | Заказ товара 0 | Заказ товара 1 | Избыток (0 / 1) |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 5 | 470 | 509 | ≈ 0 / ≈ 0 |
   | 1 | 470 | 579 | ≈ 0 / +69 |
   | 0 | 509 | 553 | +41 / +43 |
   | 4 | 575 | 625 | +107 / +115 |

   Остатки переходят в следующий цикл. Поэтому лишнее в сумме в основном остаётся неспроданным к концу или списывается и теряет полную закупочную цену: 7 за ед. товара 0 и 12 за ед. товара 1. Пока лишнее лежит, за него ещё платится хранение.

   Запас сверх спроса приносит немного. Нехватка товара 0 обходится в 8 (маржа) + 2 (неустойка), товара 1 — в 9 + 2. Перенос остатков сам гасит большую часть случайных провалов спроса.
   - У кандидата 0 избыток примерно 41 × 7 + 43 × 12 ≈ 790 закупок. Он даёт лишь около 25–30 дополнительных продаж.
   - У кандидата 4 вдобавок в день 12 склад переполняется примерно на 25 ед.: 99 ед. товара 0 плюс остатки.

3. **Устойчивость.** Кандидат 5 не упирается в вместимость склада, и его остатки не накапливаются. Если спрос окажется ниже прогноза, он теряет меньше всех. Если выше — недобирает немного, потому что неустойка всего 2.

Итог: кандидат 5 лучше всех, за ним идут 0 и 1, затем 3/6 и 2, хуже всех 4 и 7.
